note.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shells. This is why they tend to form ions in similar ways and show similar chemical properties. Group 1 metals tend to lose one electron; group 2 metals tend to lose two. Group 17 elements tend to gain one electron, while group 16 elements tend to gain two.
examples: Sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺.
Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
note.checkAnswer: A group 17 element usually gains one electron and forms a 1− anion.
note.simple: Elements in a group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they tend to react in similar ways.

written.text: Why is it not possible for oxygen atom to accept three electrons to form O³⁻ ion like nitrogen which can accept electrons to form N³⁻?

modelAnswer: Oxygen has s²,p⁴ configuration in its outermost shell, so it has six outermost-shell electrons.
It needs to accept two electrons to complete its octet.
If it accepted three electrons, it would exceed the octet.
Therefore, oxygen forms O²⁻, not O³⁻.

explain.title: Why members of a group behave alike
explain.body: The chemical properties of elements depend largely upon the number of electrons present in their outermost shells. Since in a group of the periodic table all the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell, they are expected to show similar chemical properties.

explain.title: Groups 1 and 2 lose electrons
explain.body: Group 1 elements lose one outermost electron and form positive ions. They are thus known as electropositive metals. Group 2 elements tend to lose both of their outermost electrons and form dipositive ions. The tendency to lose electrons down the group increases due to gradual increase in their atomic sizes.

explain.title: Groups 16 and 17 gain electrons
explain.body: Group 17 elements tend to gain one electron to become an anion. They are called electronegative elements. Group 16 elements tend to accept two electrons to form a dinegative ion.

explain.title: Reactivity trends
explain.body: The reactivity of alkali metals gradually increases down the group. Unlike alkali metals, the reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

explain.title: Relating group position to ion charge
explain.body: Groups 1, 2 and 3 form cations with charges 1+, 2+ and 3+ respectively. Groups 17 and 16 form anions with charges 1− and 2− respectively, as they need one or two electrons to complete their octets.

mistakes: Do not confuse the direction of the reactivity trends: alkali-metal reactivity increases down the group, but halogen reactivity decreases.
Do not give an ion charge without stating whether electrons were gained or lost.
Do not mix up group 16 and group 17: group 16 tends to gain two electrons, while group 17 tends to gain one.
Write the ion charge as a superscript-style charge, such as Mg²⁺ or Cl⁻, rather than changing the element’s subscript.
